name: Amira Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Mornings are lectures, then afternoons in the Python lab. I live in a flat two streets from campus that my dad pays for, because he owns two pharmacies and wants me to focus. Most evenings I redo the lab exercises on paper first, because I don't trust myself at the keyboard yet.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the maths module and my flatmate Dina, who studies nursing and always has stories. What wears me out is that half my course pastes questions into chatbots and gets answers in a minute. I don't use them, so I feel slow next to everyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture I'll call AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, and I'd feel a bit proved right. I'd tell Dina the panic was marketing and that learning things properly was never a waste. Online I'd stay quiet, because I don't post much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be relieved, but not fully calm. My dad pays a lot for this degree, and the pharmacies feel every price rise. If AI is hype, the real question is just whether I'm good enough to get hired.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on exactly as I am. I'd redo the lab sheets twice a week and go to the maths help hour on Thursdays. I'd also apply for a summer placement at the council's IT office, because big firms won't look at my grades.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Settled, mostly. A little embarrassed that I wanted it to be hype, because that sounds like hiding from change. But it's a nice picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd feel proved right. Is some of that about people on your course who use chatbots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, a bit. A boy in my lab group, Karim, handed in code he couldn't explain and still got a good mark. If it's hype, that stops mattering and people who learned properly come out ahead. I know that isn't very generous of me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What worry stays with you even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Getting a placement. My grades are average with no scholarship, and there are far more applicants than places. Dad says he'll call a friend, but I want my first placement to be something I earned, not something my dad arranged with a friend of his.

say: I'd say **good**, the panic was marketing and learning properly still counts.
I'd tell my flatmate Dina that I was right to keep doing the work **myself**.
think: I'm relieved, but still worried about whether my **average grades** can get me hired.
My dad pays for everything, so I feel the **pressure** not to waste it.
do: Redo **lab sheets** on paper twice a week and keep going to maths help hours.
Apply for a summer **placement** at the council IT office.
feel: Mostly **settled**, with a little guilt for wanting it to be hype.
S0.quote: I want my first placement to be something I earned, not something my dad arranged with a friend of his.
fieldNote: She wants AI to be hype because she has avoided the tools and feels behind peers.
Real worry is the **placement**, not AI: average grades, no scholarship.
Proud about earning things herself, even with a wealthy family.

steps.text: Redo each week's Python lab sheet on paper before the keyboard
Apply for the council IT office summer placement without using dad's contacts
Ask the maths tutor for Thursday help hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next picture I'll call Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's unfair. Companies will call it progress while the first jobs that vanish are the ones people like me start in. I'd tell my friends in the student union that we should push for rules before it's too late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think my course is the first place it lands. Writing code is exactly the thing they mentioned, and I'm still learning to do it slowly. If a chatbot does a junior's job, my degree starts to look like a very expensive ticket to nowhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finally sit down and try one of the tools, but with a notebook next to me so I learn what it's doing. I'd join the union's campaign on graduate jobs, and I'd ask Dad about switching to a degree with more people involved, like health technology. I'd decide by the end of this academic year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, honestly. I'm on a path I picked partly because my uncle is an engineer, and I can't tell if it's still the right one. It's hard to be angry at nobody in particular.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You haven't used the chatbots at all. What would change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A friend showed me how a chatbot wrote a whole working program in a minute and I felt sick. If it was a rule that I had to use them, I'd do it, but I'd rather companies were required to keep hiring juniors. A rule, not a favour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of your future colleagues would you worry about first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the people hired just before me, the ones who learned to code the slow way like I'm doing. Firms won't replace everyone at once. They'll just stop hiring the next group, and that's me.

say: I'd say it's **unfair**: the first jobs to go are ones like mine.
I'd push my student union to demand **rules** on graduate hiring.
think: My degree could become an expensive **ticket** to nowhere.
Firms won't fire people, they'll quietly stop **hiring** the next group, which is mine.
do: Try one **AI tool** with a notebook beside me to see how it works.
Join the union's graduate **jobs campaign** and ask Dad about changing course.
feel: **Anxious** and unsure whether I picked the right path.
S1.quote: Firms won't replace everyone at once. They'll just stop hiring the next group, and that's me.
fieldNote: Blames companies and wants regulation, in line with progressive views.
First contact with AI use: she tries tools **reluctantly**, learning not copying.
Course switch is an option she raises but hasn't decided.

steps.text: Try one AI coding tool with a notebook beside me
Join the student union campaign on graduate jobs
Ask Dad about switching to health technology by summer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next picture I'll call AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've been lied to about having time. I'd tell friends to get out of student housing deals that need three years of rent, and online I'd back anyone calling for a ban on firing people for AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm scared. I'd finish my second year in a world where my degree might not matter, with a dad who has spent years paying for it. I can't see a job at the end of it, and it's too soon for any rule or retraining plan to be ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first month I'd phone Dad and talk honestly about stopping or changing. I'd go to the careers office and ask what actually survives. I'd join every union and protest I could, because I think only crowds change things in two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. It's like standing on a platform and hearing a train, with no timetable. I'd probably not sleep for a few nights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years is very short for you. What exactly would you do in the first month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would be an awful call. I'd tell my dad I don't want to waste another year of his money on a course that may be worthless. He'd probably say finish it anyway, and I think he'd be right, but I'd still be scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your dad?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start taking pharmacy shifts at his shop. It's a job a robot won't do soon, and I'd feel useful. I'd rather hand out medicine than watch my course disappear.

say: I'd say we were **lied to** about having time.
I'd back protests and a ban on **firing for AI**.
think: I'm **scared**: my degree might not matter by the time I finish.
I can't see a job at the end, and no rule or retraining plan would be **ready**.
do: Phone Dad in the first month and talk honestly about **stopping** or changing.
Ask the careers office what survives and take **shifts** in Dad's pharmacy.
feel: **Alarmed**, like hearing a train with no timetable.
S2.quote: I'd rather hand out medicine than watch my course disappear.
fieldNote: Fear is tied to guilt about Dad's money, not only her own future.
Hands-on pharmacy shifts appeal as **safe** work she wouldn't need AI for.
Distrusts institutions and trusts mass action over quick policy.

steps.text: Phone Dad in the first month about stopping or changing degree
Ask the careers office which jobs survive
Take weekend shifts at Dad's pharmacy
Join the student union protests on AI and jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next picture I'll call AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a warning with a date, so it should mean action. I'd tell people on my course not to wait for the university to fix it. Online I'd share anything useful about graduate rules.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be worried but not panicking. I'd finish my degree in 2029, two years before AGI, so I'd be entering a job market that's already changing. That's still a hard first job to get with average grades.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use these years properly. I'd learn the tools at last and finish my degree, and I'd try for placements in public services, like hospital IT, which move slowly. I'd also save part of my allowance rather than spending it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's better than two years, but it's the sort of thing where I'd check the news every morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With five years, what would you do differently from the two-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me the degree and one proper job before the worst bit. It doesn't remove the fear, but I can plan. In the two-year picture I'm making emergency decisions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you blame most in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big tech firms and the investors behind them, mostly. They'll get the money and the rest of us get told to retrain. I'd blame the people who set the rules too, for letting it run.

say: I'd call it a **warning with a date**, so people should act now.
I'd tell classmates not to wait for the **university** to fix it.
think: I'd finish in 2029, just **before** AGI, into a job market already shifting.
Average grades make a **first job** hard even before AGI.
do: Learn the AI tools while studying and aim for **hospital IT** placements.
Save part of my **allowance** instead of spending it.
S3.quote: Five years gives me the degree and one proper job before the worst bit. It doesn't remove the fear, but I can plan.
fieldNote: Five years lets her plan, which calms her compared with the **two-year** picture.
Blame is aimed at tech firms, investors and rule-makers.
Public-sector placements seem safer to her than start-ups.

steps.text: Learn two AI coding tools properly over the next year
Save half of each month's allowance
Apply for hospital and council IT placements

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next picture I'll call AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the best of the three, because a decade is a real plan. I'd tell younger students to pick something they like, since nobody can say what will be safe. I'd stay calm online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel almost okay. I'd be 28 when AGI arrives, with years of work, a bit of savings and maybe a union behind me. Ten years is enough to get skills nobody can easily copy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, learn the tools, and aim for work with people involved, maybe technical support in hospitals. I'd keep a savings habit and vote for parties that talk about retraining and income help. I wouldn't change course unless something really forced me to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a little worry at the edges. It feels like a long road, and long roads let you adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, is your degree still the right choice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I think so. A decade is enough time to try a placement, find out what I like and change if I need to. The degree isn't a waste, it's a starting point.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your dad and Dina say to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dad would say finish it and keep learning, because pharmacies change too. Dina would say care work isn't going anywhere and I could always come into it. They'd both be kind, and that matters more than the argument.

say: I'd say this is the best of the three because a **decade** is a real plan.
I'd tell younger students to pick what they **like**.
think: At 28 I'd have **years** of work, savings and a union behind me.
Ten years is enough to build **skills** nobody can easily copy.
do: Finish the **degree**, learn the tools and aim for people-facing technical work.
Build a **savings** habit and vote for retraining and income support.
feel: Mostly **calm**, with some worry at the edges.
S4.quote: A decade is enough time to try a placement, find out what I like and change if I need to.
fieldNote: Her calm grows with time; she **adjusts** best when she has a long runway.
Family and flatmate support her, even if she is reluctant to rely on it.
Still prefers people-facing work as the safe choice.

steps.text: Finish the degree and aim for hospital technical support work
Put a fixed amount into savings every month
Vote for parties offering retraining and income support

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year picture, by far. My degree would be half done, my dad would have spent a fortune, and nothing would be ready. What would help is time, a rule that companies keep hiring graduates, and someone in the university telling us honestly what survives.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not as against AI as I sound. I'm slow with AI tools because I'm scared of getting them wrong. If somebody patient showed me how to use it without copying, I think I'd like it.

headlineQuote: I'm slow with AI tools because I'm scared of getting them wrong.
portrait: **Amira** is 18, a first-year software engineering student with an average school record and a dad who owns two pharmacies.
She avoids AI tools, redoes lab work by hand and feels slow beside classmates who use chatbots.
Her worry grows with speed: **uneasy** with hype or a decade, anxious with five years, alarmed with two.
She blames tech firms and wants union action and rules, and sees pharmacy work as a safe fallback.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture worries her most: half a degree, a fortune spent, and nothing ready.
whatWouldHelp: **Time**, a rule that companies keep hiring graduates, and honest advice from her university about what survives.
